criterion_notes.c1: Examines community-level drinking water and sanitation service access (coverage of Water Supply Systems [WSS/SAA], treated water, and domestic Sanitary Modules [SM]) across Indigenous villages in Tocantins, Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision: include) because it reviews Brazil's legal, institutional, and policy framework for Indigenous health and sanitation (PNASPI / Ordinance 254/2002, SasiSUS / Law 9,836/1999, SESAI and DSEI-TO / Law 12,314/2010, Basic Sanitation Laws 11,445/2007 and 14,026/2020, and Ordinance GM/MS 888/2021) and evaluates policy implementation deficits in Indigenous territories. Fails the active narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2 (c2_legal_admin_factor: no): the study does not empirically analyze any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, official discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Instead, PNASPI and related statutes serve as uniform macro-governance and generic public-program delivery background across all DSEI-TO villages, juxtaposed only with descriptive cross-sectional counts of village infrastructure by ethnicity (Table 3) and acute diarrheal disease cases by infrastructure category (Table 4), plus normative calls for culturally sensitive participatory governance.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains empirical secondary administrative/surveillance data from official SESAI/SIASI databases (Brasil, 2019) covering Indigenous villages in Tocantins (Tables 3 and 4), combined with a PRISMA-framed systematic literature review (44 articles narratively discussed) and a national legislative/policy review (Table 2). Although a Methods subheading mentions primary data collection and chi-square/t-tests, the reported village evidence consists solely of descriptive secondary tabulations.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports measurable community and population service-access outcomes in Table 3: proportion and count of Indigenous villages and residents with both Water Supply Systems (WSS) and domestic Sanitary Modules (SM) (17 villages, 10.6%), water treatment/WSS only without SM (93 villages, 58%), and lacking both treated water and SM (51 villages, 31.8%), alongside acute diarrheal disease (ADD) incidence in Table 4.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (Indigenous villages [160 in text; 161 in Table 3] and residents [11,908 in text; 11,688 in Table 3] in DSEI-TO, Tocantins), outcomes (WSS and SM access; ADD incidence), macro-policy context / infrastructure strata, and study design (descriptive cross-sectional secondary-data policy evaluation with literature and legislative review) are identifiable, though no rule-type legal/administrative exposure varies or is tested.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with English and Portuguese abstracts), which is directly eligible without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study analyzes the implementation and effectiveness of water supply and sanitation policies targeting Indigenous peoples, with an emphasis on the National Indigenous Peoples Health Policy (PNASPI).

The methodology adopted combined a systematic review of literature, national legislation, and health policy documents with the analysis of sanitation infrastructure data from 160 Indigenous villages, sourced from official databases.
The results show that only 10% of villages have both water supply systems and sanitary modules, while 30% of the Indigenous population lacks treated water, violating PNASPI provisions.
Secondary data were extracted from the Special Secretariat for Indigenous Health (SESAI) reports and health information systems available on the Virtual Health Library (VHL) platform (Brasil, 2019).
93 (58%) have water treatment plants without sanitary modules, and 51 (31.8%) lack access to treated water and sanitary modules

Upon scrutinizing the data (Table 3), it becomes clear that the National Policy for Health Care for Indigenous Peoples (PNASPI) (Brasil, 2002) has not been effectively implemented, despite providing for a complementary service organization model.

raw_response.exposure: National Indigenous health and sanitation macro-policy framework (PNASPI, SasiSUS, SESAI/DSEI-TO, Laws 11,445/2007 and 14,026/2020) treated as uniform policy-implementation background; village sanitation infrastructure category (WSS and SM) for diarrheal disease comparison
raw_response.outcome: Village-level and population-level coverage of Water Supply Systems (WSS), treated water, and domestic Sanitary Modules (SM) (Table 3), and incidence of acute diarrheal disease (ADD) (Table 4)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Indigenous communities in the Special Indigenous Health District of Tocantins (DSEI-TO), Tocantins, Brazil: 160 villages and 11,908 residents across nine ethnic groups reported in text (161 villages and 11,688 residents across five ethnic groups tabulated in Table 3 from 2019 SESAI/SIASI data); 44 peer-reviewed studies in literature review
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study reports empirical secondary administrative data (SESAI/SIASI, 2019) on drinking-water supply systems and domestic sanitary modules across Indigenous villages in Tocantins, Brazil (satisfying c1, c3, and c4), it does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, administrative burden, tariffs, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory/ownership structure). Instead, Brazilian national policies (PNASPI, SasiSUS, SESAI, and the Basic Sanitation Laws) are discussed as uniform macro-governance and generic policy-implementation background alongside descriptive tabulations of infrastructure coverage by ethnicity (Table 3) and diarrheal disease by infrastructure status (Table 4). Under the broad plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper would have been included as an evaluation of Indigenous sanitation policy implementation.
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive cross-sectional analysis of secondary administrative data (SESAI/SIASI) combined with a systematic literature review and legislative/policy document review
